questions.prompt: How dense is a neutron star compared with ordinary matter?
options: About as dense as granite
About as dense as gold
A sugar-cube-size piece weighs about a billion tonnes
Only slightly denser than water
questions.explanation: Two solar masses packed into a 20-km ball means a sugar cube of neutron matter weighs roughly a billion tonnes — a mountain in your hand.
questions.misconception: Everything you've touched is ordinary matter, so 'very dense' usually means gold or lead — but those are still almost entirely empty space compared with the neutron lattice of a collapsed star.

questions.prompt: What keeps a neutron star from collapsing into a black hole?
options: Fusion fires in its center
Neutrons packed to the quantum limit push back — neutron degeneracy pressure
A solid iron frame inside
Its spin flings gravity away
questions.explanation: Like electrons in a white dwarf, neutrons cannot be squeezed into the same quantum state. Packed that tight, they push back hard enough to hold up roughly two solar masses — for now.
questions.misconception: The word 'collapse' makes it sound like it happens instantly; but the collapse only stops when the matter is squeezed into its absolute limit — and the limit of that squeeze is what 'degeneracy' names.

questions.prompt: A neutron star is the leftover of which event?
options: A red giant puffing off a nebula
A supernova — the explosion of a very massive star
A planet crash
Two white dwarfs cooling together
questions.explanation: Stars with at least about eight solar masses end in a supernova whose core collapses into a neutron star — the explosion's debris cloud surrounds the new remnant.
questions.misconception: After the white dwarf's gentle planetary nebula, it is easy to assume every star's end is soft — but the neutron star is born in the most violent event the star will ever have.

questions.prompt: Why does a pulsar seem to flash at perfectly regular intervals?
options: It blinks like a signal light on purpose
Radio beams from its poles sweep past Earth with every rotation, like a lighthouse
It is actually a hole opening and closing
Its fusion reignites every few seconds
questions.explanation: The magnetic poles spit out narrow beams. As the star rotates up to hundreds of times per second, each beam swings across Earth like a lighthouse beam — giving the clock-like ticking.
questions.misconception: A steady pulse naturally reads as a deliberate signal — in 1967 the discoverers even jokingly named it LGM-1, 'Little Green Men', before concluding it was a rotating remnant.

questions.prompt: Why does a neutron star spin so fast?
options: A supernova gives it a push like a kick
Its magnetic field accelerates it later
When the huge star's core shrinks from ~1,000 km to ~20 km, spin speeds up like a skater pulling in her arms
It does not spin fast — telescopes only look at it briefly
questions.explanation: Angular momentum is conserved: the collapsing core pulls its mass inward, and the same total spin wrapped into a tiny radius must spin much faster — from maybe one rotation a day to dozens per second.
questions.misconception: It feels like the explosion should provide the speed; in reality the pre-explosion star's own slow rotation is amplified by the shrink — the same trick a spinning skater performs.
